967.title: Five steps
967.hook: psychologist Everett Worthington's REACH model: recall, empathize, give the gift, commit, hold on
967.howItsDone: Psychologists who use Everett Worthington's REACH model usually teach it in groups or workbooks, taking people through recall, empathy, the gift of forgiveness, a commitment and holding on, one step at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shu: what you don't want done to you, don't do to others. Your line was stand where they stood. Today the theme turns from the old voices to what science and history can say.

A psychologist spends his working life studying forgiveness. He builds a method, teaches it in workshops, writes it up in books. Then life tests the method on him. Everett Worthington has written that after his mother was killed in a break-in at her home, he found himself walking through his own steps, one by one, to see whether they would hold for the person who had built them. They weren't a theory anymore. The method's name is five letters, R, E, A, C, H, and each letter is a step.
screen: `A PSYCHOLOGIST STUDIES FORGIVENESS.` → `LIFE TESTS HIS METHOD.` → `FIVE LETTERS: REACH.`

segments.voice: R is recall: remember the hurt as plainly as you can, without turning the other person into a monster or yourself into nothing but a victim. Just what happened. E is empathize: try to see the one who hurt you from the inside. What fear, pressure or story might they have been carrying that day? This step has old company. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, wrote in his private notebook, in George Long's translation: "When a man has done thee any wrong, immediately consider with what opinion about good or evil he has done wrong." The emperor and the psychologist point the same way: understanding comes before letting go. And understanding is not agreeing. A is the altruistic gift. Worthington asks people to remember a time they themselves were forgiven, then offer forgiveness the way a gift is offered, freely, not because it was earned. C is commit: say it to a friend, or write it down, so the decision has a shape outside your head. H is hold on. The hurt can come back, and in Worthington's telling that isn't proof the forgiveness failed. It's a moment to return to what you decided. You don't have to climb all five at once. A person can stand on recall a long while, or find empathy the steepest stair. It's a staircase, not an exam, and any single stair is a real place to stand.
screen: `R: RECALL IT PLAINLY.` · `E: SEE THEM FROM THE INSIDE.` · `A, C: A GIFT, THEN A COMMITMENT.` · `H: HOLD ON WHEN IT COMES BACK.` · then, large: `CONSIDER WITH WHAT OPINION HE HAS DONE WRONG.`

segments.voice: Choose one modest hurt and one step only: for recall, tell yourself what happened in two plain sentences with no villain in them; for empathy, ask what that person might have been carrying that day; for the gift, remember one time someone let you off. Stay with that single step while the breath comes and goes; the top of the staircase can wait.
Five steps. Recall, empathize, give the gift, commit, hold on: Everett Worthington's REACH, a staircase you can climb one stair at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one step. One stair is still a stair. Nine hundred sixty-seven days now.

968.title: The forgiveness project
968.hook: Fred Luskin's Stanford work taught people to change the story they tell about a hurt
968.howItsDone: In forgiveness workshops based on Fred Luskin's approach, people write or speak their grievance story, look at the rules they expected others to follow, and practice telling the story again with themselves as the one who came through it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was five steps: Everett Worthington's REACH. Recall, empathize, give the gift, commit, hold on. Your line was one step.

A grievance often comes with a script. Somebody at dinner asks what happened with the old roommate, or a boss from a job long gone, and the story rolls out the same way it did last time: the same villain, the same turning point, the same ending, word for word, like a song on repeat. Fred Luskin, a psychologist at Stanford, gave that script a name: the grievance story. In the Stanford Forgiveness Project he taught people to notice how they tell their stories, and then to try telling them a different way.
screen: `A STORY ON REPEAT.` → `LUSKIN NAMES IT.` → `TELL IT ANOTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Luskin reports in his book Forgive for Good that people who went through his forgiveness training came out with less hurt and less anger than before. Not none. Less. That's the modest, honest claim, and it's the one to keep. In Luskin's account, a story told often enough becomes a groove. Each retelling walks the same path and wears it a little deeper. He also points to what he calls unenforceable rules: things we expect from other people that we have no power to make them do. Be fair to me. Never lie to me. Remember my birthday. Good hopes, all of them. But when a rule can't be enforced, the hurt keeps going off every time it's broken, like an alarm nobody can reach. An old voice says something close. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher, put it this way in George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The thing that happened stays what it was. What can move is the opinion laid over it. So Luskin invites people to retell the same story with themselves cast differently: not only as the one it happened to, but as the one who came through it and is still learning. The facts don't change. The villain is still in the story. What changes is where the story ends, and who's at the center when it does.
screen: `THE GRIEVANCE STORY.` · `RULES NO ONE CAN ENFORCE.` · `NOT THE THING, THE OPINION.` · `THE SAME FACTS, A NEW CENTER.` · then, large: `LESS HURT, NOT NO HURT.`

segments.voice: Bring up one grievance you've told more than once, and retell it kindly in three plain sentences: what happened, what it cost, and what you've done since and know now. Keep the other person in it, no nicer than they were; just let the last sentence be about you moving, and say it once more, slowly.
Luskin. The Stanford psychologist who taught people to notice their grievance story and tell it another way. Today's word.
Your line: less hurt. Not no hurt; less, and the facts stay the same. See you tomorrow.

969.title: Not reconciling
969.hook: forgiving doesn't require going back to the relationship
969.howItsDone: Some counselors who work with forgiveness separate it from reconciliation: a person may forgive privately, in writing that is never sent or in prayer, without restoring contact.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Luskin, who taught people to tell the grievance story with a new center. Your line was less hurt.

Two brothers meet on a road. Jacob, the younger, once tricked Esau out of their father's blessing and ran for his life. Now he is coming home, bracing for the worst. And Genesis says: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." A few weeks back, this path stood with Esau as he ran. Today, read on to the end of the chapter. The chapter keeps going. Esau offers to travel on together. Jacob gently says no. And the two brothers take two different roads.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS MEET.` → `AN EMBRACE, AND TEARS.` → `THEN TWO ROADS.`

segments.voice: The psychology of forgiveness draws a line here. Everett Worthington, whose five steps came two days ago, titled one of his books Forgiving and Reconciling, and he treats them as two different things. Forgiving can happen inside one person. Reconciling takes two, and it needs trust to be rebuilt, which takes behavior over time from both sides. You can do the first alone, not the second. Back to Genesis. After the embrace, Jacob says his children are young and his flocks are slow, and he'll follow at their pace. Esau goes home to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth. The text doesn't tell us why Jacob holds back. Some readers hear caution; some hear wisdom; some hear a man who still can't quite believe he's forgiven. What the story does show is an embrace that is real and a distance that stays. An older pair in the same book: when the herdsmen of Abram, as Abraham is still called there, keep quarreling with his nephew Lot's herdsmen, Abram says: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee." And his answer to keeping the peace is space: "separate thyself, I pray thee, from me." Peace, kept by distance. Some relationships can be rebuilt, and that can be good. Others shouldn't be, because going back would mean walking into the same harm. Forgiveness, as Worthington describes it, doesn't ask anyone to walk back in. It can be done from across a field.
screen: `FORGIVING AND RECONCILING: TWO THINGS.` · `AN EMBRACE, THEN TWO ROADS.` · `NO STRIFE, AND SEPARATE LAND.` · `NO ONE HAS TO WALK BACK INTO HARM.` · then, large: `FROM A DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're no longer close to, or don't want to be close to again, and leave them where they are, small and far away across a wide field. From where you sit, let the rope between you go slack: you're not walking over or calling them, only letting go of your end. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer from right where you are; the gap stays.
Not reconciling. Forgiving can happen inside one person; reconciling takes two and rebuilt trust. You can forgive and still keep the distance. Today's word.
Your line: from a distance. The embrace was real, and so was the road apart. Day nine hundred sixty-nine, done.

970.title: Not excusing
970.hook: forgiving doesn't mean it was okay
970.howItsDone: In forgiveness counseling based on Robert Enright's work, people first name the wrong done to them and the harm it caused, and only then consider forgiving; forgiveness is taught as distinct from condoning, excusing or forgetting.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not reconciling: Jacob and Esau embraced, wept, and then took two different roads. Your line was from a distance.

"It's fine." Two small words. Someone apologizes for the missed birthday, the sharp comment in the meeting, the promise that quietly fell through, and out comes the reflex: it's fine, don't worry about it. Sometimes that's simply true. Sometimes it's a way to end an awkward moment and get back to dinner. And sometimes it isn't fine at all, and saying so would feel like making a scene. Forgiving someone and telling them it was fine can sound almost the same out loud. Today pulls them apart.
screen: `IT'S FINE.` → `SOMETIMES IT ISN'T.` → `TWO THINGS THAT SOUND ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Robert Enright, a psychologist who has written about forgiveness, sets out what forgiveness is not. It is not condoning. It is not excusing. It is not forgetting. His point is almost a matter of logic: you can only forgive something that was actually wrong. If it was fine, there's nothing to forgive. An old story does this out loud. In Genesis, Joseph's brothers once sold him away. Years later he has power over them, and after their father dies they're terrified he'll finally take revenge. Listen to the order of what he says: "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." He names it first, plainly, to their faces. He doesn't say it was nothing. Then, in the next verse: "Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones." Named, and then let go. Why the naming matters: excusing makes the wrong smaller until it disappears. Forgiving lets the wrong keep its full size, and releases it anyway. That's harder, and more honest, because the person who was hurt doesn't have to pretend. On an ordinary Tuesday it sounds like two sentences, both true, said together: that wasn't okay, and I'm letting it go. Neither cancels the other. The first protects the truth. The second frees the one saying it.
screen: `NOT CONDONING, EXCUSING, FORGETTING.` · `YE THOUGHT EVIL AGAINST ME.` · `FULL SIZE, THEN LET GO.` · `TWO TRUE SENTENCES AT ONCE.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T OKAY.`

segments.voice: Choose one wrong done to you that you've waved away with "it's fine," and name it in one plain sentence in your head: what they did, and that it wasn't okay, at full size, with no speech. Let it stand for a few breaths, then, if you're ready, add the second sentence, and I'm letting it go; if you're not ready, the first sentence is enough for today.
Not excusing. Forgiving lets a wrong keep its full size and releases it anyway; excusing shrinks it to nothing. Today's word.
Your line: it wasn't okay. Both sentences can be true at once. That's day nine hundred seventy.

971.title: Not yet
971.hook: rushing forgiveness can hurt; healing keeps its own time
971.howItsDone: Forgiveness counselors who follow Robert Enright's process model begin by helping people uncover the hurt and anger, and let the decision to forgive come later, in its own time.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not excusing: Joseph named the evil first, to his brothers' faces, and then let it go. Your line was it wasn't okay.

A broken wrist goes into a cast, and nobody asks it to throw a ball the next morning. Everyone can see the plaster. Everyone understands the bone needs time, and that pushing it too soon can break it again. Hurts of the heart don't come with a cast. Nobody can see them, so forgiveness sometimes gets asked for on a schedule: at the funeral, across the holiday table, the day after the apology, by someone who means well and wants things smooth again.
screen: `A CAST ON A BROKEN WRIST.` → `HEART HURTS HAVE NO CAST.` → `FORGIVENESS ON A SCHEDULE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes, the Bible's book of seasons, opens its list of times this way: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." And on that list, among planting and building and dancing, is this: "a time to heal." Not a moment. A time. Healing gets its own season, and the list doesn't say how long a season is. Robert Enright, whose list came yesterday, describes forgiveness as a process with phases, and his first phase is uncovering: looking honestly at the hurt and the anger before trying to do anything with them. That order matters. It's hard to release something you haven't looked at yet. A forgiveness pushed out too early, to keep the peace or please someone else, can turn into a lid on the hurt rather than a release of it. The words get said; the wound underneath can stay open. That's why, in Enright's order, the looking comes first. Then a line from the Psalms: "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds." Healing comes with binding up: the wound is wrapped and given time. A bandage isn't a refusal to get better; it's part of how getting better happens. So not yet isn't the opposite of forgiveness. It can be the first part of it. Not yet is not never. It's a cast on the wrist while the bone does its slow, invisible work.
screen: `A TIME TO HEAL.` · `UNCOVER BEFORE YOU RELEASE.` · `A LID IS NOT A RELEASE.` · `NOT YET IS NOT NEVER.` · then, large: `HE BINDETH UP THEIR WOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Choose one hurt that's still fresh, one you're not ready to forgive, and instead of forgiving it, sit beside it the way you'd sit beside a friend in a cast: not fixing, not pushing, just keeping it company, with a hand on your chest or lap if that helps. In your head, say two words to it, not yet, and let that be enough for the whole sit.
Not yet. A time to heal comes before a time to let go; not yet can be the first part of forgiveness, not its opposite. Today's word.
Your line: not yet is allowed. Healing keeps its own season, however long that is. See you tomorrow.

972.title: Truth and reconciliation
972.hook: South Africa's commission heard victims and perpetrators after apartheid, imperfectly and bravely
972.howItsDone: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission held public hearings where people harmed under apartheid gave testimony, and separate amnesty hearings where applicants had to disclose fully the politically motivated crimes they had committed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not yet: a time to heal, and a cast on the wrist while the bone does its slow work. Your line was not yet is allowed.

A table, a row of microphones, a room full of listeners. People who had been harmed sit down and, in public, say what was done to them and to the people they loved. In other hearings, people who had done harm sit at a table too, and describe what they did. This was South Africa, after apartheid ended, and the body holding the hearings was the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Two words in its name, in a particular order.
screen: `THE HARMED TELL WHAT HAPPENED.` → `THOSE WHO HARMED DESCRIBE IT.` → `TRUTH, THEN RECONCILIATION.`

segments.voice: At its center was an unusual trade. The law that set up the commission allowed people who had committed politically motivated crimes to apply for amnesty. But there was a condition: they had to tell the full truth about what they had done. Not a vague regret. The full account. Truth was the price of amnesty. Look again at the name. Truth comes first, and reconciliation second. For a family that had never been told what happened to someone they loved, or who gave the order, or where a body lay, hearing it said out loud could matter more than anything else the commission could offer. Reconciliation, if it came, would have to stand on that. Tutu kept returning to an idea in his book No Future Without Forgiveness: ubuntu, a word from southern Africa for the belief that a person is a person through other people. Who I am is bound up with who you are. In Tutu's telling, that's why forgiveness wasn't soft or optional for a nation. If my humanity is bound to yours, your cruelty diminishes me, and your healing is part of mine. And honesty about the result: it was imperfect, and people in South Africa and beyond still argue about what it achieved and what it left undone, about justice, about repair, about who never came forward. The bravery and the arguing are both part of the story. On a smaller scale it still holds: before anyone talks about moving on, the truth of what happened gets said, plainly, and heard.
screen: `AMNESTY FOR THE FULL TRUTH.` · `TRUTH COMES FIRST IN THE NAME.` · `UBUNTU: A PERSON THROUGH PEOPLE.` · `BRAVE, IMPERFECT, STILL ARGUED.` · then, large: `TRUTH FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hurt, one you received or one you caused, where the plain truth of what happened has never quite been said. Don't say it now, and don't plan a conversation; just let the truth be fully true inside you for these few minutes, without softening it.
Ubuntu. Desmond Tutu's word for the belief that a person is a person through other people, at the heart of South Africa's truth commission. Today's word.
Your line: truth first. Reconciliation, if it comes, stands on it. Day nine hundred seventy-two, done.

973.title: Restorative justice
973.hook: bringing together those harmed and those who harmed, to repair
973.howItsDone: In restorative justice programs, a trained facilitator brings together, when both agree, the person harmed and the person responsible, so that the harm can be described and a plan for repair agreed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ubuntu: a person is a person through other people. Your line was truth first.

"Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Nobody asked Zacchaeus for that sentence. Three weeks ago this path climbed the sycamore in Jericho with him, the rich tax collector Jesus called down by name. Today, look only at what he stands up and says, and read it as a plan. Not only sorry. Restore.
screen: `BACK TO THE SYCAMORE.` → `A SENTENCE NOBODY ASKED FOR.` → `I RESTORE HIM FOURFOLD.`

segments.voice: Howard Zehr, who has written about restorative justice, points out that a courtroom usually asks: what law was broken, who did it, and what do they deserve? Restorative justice asks different questions: who has been hurt, what do they need, and whose obligation is it to meet those needs? The center moves from the broken rule to the harmed person. Where both sides agree to it, the people harmed and the person who harmed meet, with someone guiding the conversation. The harmed person can say what happened to them and ask what they need to ask. The one who did harm hears it face to face, not from behind a lawyer. Then together they work out what repair could be. Now Zacchaeus again. What he offers isn't a feeling, and it isn't a punishment someone hands him. It's repair, aimed at the specific people he took from, and more than he took. Step back and look at the whole week. It began inside one person, with Worthington's five steps and Luskin's grievance story. Then it marked the edges: forgiving isn't reconciling, it isn't excusing, and it's allowed to say not yet. Then the circle widened: a nation telling the truth in public, and now a room where harm and repair sit at the same table. From a single heart out to a whole community, and the question kept getting more practical. What would make this right?
screen: `WHO WAS HURT? WHAT DO THEY NEED?` · `THE HARMED AND THE HARMER MEET.` · `REPAIR, NOT ONLY SORRY.` · `A WEEK: FROM ONE HEART OUTWARD.` · then, large: `I RESTORE HIM FOURFOLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one harm, one you did or one done to you, and ask Zehr's questions quietly, one at a time: who was hurt, what do they need, and whose job is it to meet that need? Then let the shape of repair come clear, something returned, a story corrected, time given back, without needing to do it yet.
Restorative justice. Bringing together those harmed and those who harmed, asking who was hurt and what they need, and working toward repair. Today's word.
Your line: repair. Not only sorry, but something actually made right. Nine hundred seventy-three days in.
